content.text: Unit 2 Overview

Unit 2 is about how computers represent, store, compress, and process data. It covers four topics: Binary Numbers (2.1), Data Compression (2.2), Extracting Information from Data (2.3), and Using Programs with Data (2.4). This unit accounts for 17–22% of the AP exam — one of the heavier units. The central ideas are that everything in a computer is ultimately bits, and that programs can be used to process data to discover information and create new knowledge.

content.label: Big Ideas
content.text:
DAT-1: The way a computer represents data internally is different from the way the data are interpreted and displayed for the user. Programs are used to translate data into a representation more easily understood by people.

DAT-2: Programs can be used to process data, which allows users to discover information and create new knowledge.
Topic 2.1 — How Computers Represent Data with Bits

content.definition: Short for binary digit. The lowest-level component of any value in a computing device. A bit is either 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits.

content.text: Computing devices represent data digitally — meaning the lowest-level components of any value are bits. Data values can be stored in variables, lists of items, or standalone constants, and can be passed as input to or output from procedures. Everything a computer does — displaying text, playing music, running a program — ultimately comes down to manipulating sequences of 0s and 1s.
Topic 2.1 — Abstraction: How Bits Represent Everything

content.definition: The process of reducing complexity by focusing on the main idea. Bits are grouped to represent abstractions including numbers, characters, and color. The same sequence of bits may represent different types of data in different contexts.

content.text: Bits are grouped to represent abstractions — including numbers, characters, and color. By grouping bits, computers can represent anything from a letter of the alphabet to a pixel in a photo to a financial transaction. The same sequence of bits may represent completely different types of data depending on how the program interprets them.

rows: 65 (decimal)
Letter 'A' (ASCII)
65 out of 255 in an RGB value
255 (decimal)
Non-printable character
Maximum intensity — full red, green, or blue in RGB
0 (decimal)
Null character
0 — no intensity for that color channel

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The same sequence of bits can mean completely different things depending on context — this is one of the most tested concepts in Unit 2. 01000001 is 65 as a number, 'A' as text, and a color component depending on how the program interprets it. The bits themselves don't carry inherent meaning — the context does.
Topic 2.1 — Analog vs Digital Data

content.definition: Analog data changes smoothly and continuously over time. Digital data represents values in discrete bits. Using digital data to approximate analog data is an example of abstraction. Sampling is used to digitally approximate analog data.
Measuring values of an analog signal at regular intervals to approximate it digitally. The samples are measured to determine the exact bits required to store each sample.

rows: Values change smoothly and continuously — infinite possible values between any two points
Values are represented in discrete bits — finite possible values
Cannot be stored directly in a computer
Can be stored, transmitted, and processed by computers
Examples: pitch of a voice, volume of music, position of a sprinter, colors of a painting
Examples: MP3 audio file, digital photo, temperature stored as a number in memory
Perfectly captures every nuance of the real world
Approximates the real world — some precision is always lost through sampling

content.text: Using digital data to approximate real-world analog data is itself an example of abstraction. The digital version hides the infinite detail of the analog signal and represents only what was captured at the sampling intervals. A higher sampling rate (more samples per second) produces a closer approximation — but it is always an approximation, never a perfect copy.
Topic 2.1 — The Binary Number System

content.definition: A base-2 number system using only 0 and 1. Place values are powers of 2 starting at 1 on the right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... A digit's value equals the bit multiplied by its place value.
Multiply each bit by its place value (power of 2) and add the results. Example: 1101 = (1×8) + (1×4) + (0×2) + (1×1) = 13.

content.text: The place value of each position is determined by the base (2) raised to the power of the position. Positions are numbered starting at 0 on the rightmost digit, increasing by 1 to the left. So place values from right to left are: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128...

content.code:
Binary to Decimal — Example 1:
  1  1  0  1
  ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓
  8  4  2  1   ← place values
  8  4  0  1   ← bit × place value
  8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13

Binary to Decimal — Example 2:
  1  0  1  1  0
  ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓
  16 8  4  2  1  ← place values
  16 0  4  2  0  ← bit × place value
  16 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 22

Decimal to Binary — Example:
  13 ÷ 2 = 6  R 1  ← least significant bit
   6 ÷ 2 = 3  R 0
   3 ÷ 2 = 1  R 1
   1 ÷ 2 = 0  R 1  ← most significant bit
  Read remainders bottom to top: 1101
  So decimal 13 = binary 1101 ✓

content.text: Topic 2.1 — Errors from Fixed-Bit Representation

content.definition: Occurs when a computer attempts to handle a number outside the defined range of values. Caused by the fixed number of bits used to represent integers in many programming languages.
Occurs because the fixed number of bits used to represent real numbers limits precision. Some real numbers can only be stored as approximations.

rows: Overflow error
A result exceeds the maximum or minimum value storable in the fixed number of bits
Integers (whole numbers)
Variable holding 0–255 tries to store 300 → overflow error
Round-off error
Fixed bits cannot represent all decimal values with exact precision
Real numbers (decimals)
Storing 1/3 results in 0.3333333 — an approximation

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: In the AP CSP reference sheet language, integers are limited only by the computer's memory size — not a fixed bit count. This means overflow errors don't occur for integers in AP pseudocode. But real number precision limits still apply. On the real exam, overflow is more likely to be tested in the context of other programming languages.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Overflow error = number is outside the defined RANGE (too big). Round-off error = number cannot be represented with exact PRECISION (decimal approximation). These affect different types of numbers and occur for different reasons. Know the distinction.
Topic 2.2 — Data Compression

content.definition: Reducing the size (number of bits) of transmitted or stored data. Fewer bits does not necessarily mean less information. The amount of reduction depends on the redundancy in the original data and the algorithm applied.

Lossless: guarantees complete reconstruction of original data. Best when quality matters (text, medical images).
Lossy: reconstructs only an approximation, greater size reduction. Best when minimizing file size matters (music, video, photos).

rows: Can reconstruct original exactly?
Yes — completely and perfectly
No — only an approximation
Size reduction amount?
Moderate — limited by removable redundancy
Much greater — permanently discards some data
Best when...
Quality or exact reconstruction is maximally important
Minimizing data size or transmission time is maximally important
After decompression you get...
The exact original file — bit for bit identical
An approximation — the discarded data is gone permanently
Examples
ZIP, PNG, FLAC, text files, source code
MP3, JPEG, MPEG, streaming video
Use cases
Legal documents, medical scans, program code
Music streaming, video calls, social media photos
Patient X-ray image for medical diagnosis
Lossless
Quality and exact reconstruction are maximally important — any loss could cause a missed diagnosis
Music files for a streaming service
Lossy
Minimizing file size matters most — subtle audio differences are inaudible on typical speakers
Legal contract archived for future reference
Lossless
Must be retrievable exactly as written — a single changed character could alter legal meaning
Video for a social media post
Lossy
Fast upload and smooth playback matter more than perfect video quality
Source code for a program
Lossless
Even one changed bit could introduce a syntax error that breaks the program
Live sports stream
Lossy
Transmission speed is critical — slight quality reduction is acceptable for smooth live viewing

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: When the exam gives you a compression scenario, ask: does the data NEED to be exactly reconstructed? If yes → lossless. Is minimizing size more important than quality? If yes → lossy. Remember: lossy compression permanently removes data — once gone, it cannot be recovered.
Topic 2.3 — Extracting Information from Data

content.definition: The collection of facts and patterns extracted from data. Data provide opportunities for identifying trends, making connections, and addressing problems.

Correlation: two variables appear related in data. Causation: one variable directly causes the other. A correlation found in data does NOT automatically mean causation — additional research is needed.

content.text: Digitally processed data may show a correlation between variables — meaning two things appear to change together. But a correlation found in data does not necessarily indicate that a causal relationship exists. This is one of the most important and frequently tested distinctions in AP CSP.

rows: Students who eat breakfast score higher on tests
Eating breakfast CAUSES higher test scores
There is a CORRELATION — additional research is needed to determine if causation exists
Ice cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer
Ice cream CAUSES drowning
There is a CORRELATION — both are likely caused by a third factor (hot weather)
Cities with more libraries have lower crime rates
Libraries REDUCE crime
There is a CORRELATION — the relationship needs further research
Users who post more frequently have more followers
Posting more CAUSES more followers
There is a CORRELATION — the direction and cause of the relationship is unclear

content.definition: Data about data. Example: a photo is the data; its metadata includes date taken and file size. Used for finding, organizing, and managing information. Changes to metadata do not change the primary data.

rows: A photo
Date taken, GPS location, camera model, file size, resolution
Sort photos by date; find photos from a specific location; organize by camera
An email
Sender, recipient, timestamp, subject, read/unread status
Search inbox by sender; filter by date; find unread messages
A music file
Artist, album, track number, duration, genre, year
Create playlists by genre; sort library by artist; find songs by year
A document
Author, creation date, last modified, word count, file size
Find documents by author; sort by last modified; identify recently edited files

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Changes to metadata do NOT change the primary data. Renaming a photo changes the file name (metadata) — the actual image pixels are completely unchanged. This is directly tested: 'A user changes the file name of a photo. Which of the following changes?' Answer: only the metadata changes.

content.definition: The need to clean data, incomplete data, invalid data, and the need to combine data sources. These challenges exist regardless of size. Large data sets may require parallel systems. Bias is not eliminated by collecting more data.
Making data uniform without changing its meaning. Example: replacing all equivalent abbreviations, spellings, and capitalizations with the same word.

rows: Need to clean data
Same thing recorded different ways — data is not uniform
Favorite color survey returns 'blue', 'Blue', 'BLUE', 'blu' — all the same color
Standardize all equivalent values to one format
Incomplete data
Records with missing required fields
Student database has 200 records but 30 are missing grade level
Exclude incomplete records or estimate missing values
Invalid data
Impossible or clearly wrong values
Age field contains '247' or '-5'
Identify and remove or correct invalid entries
Need to combine sources
One source doesn't contain all needed data
Traffic cameras show WHERE congestion is but not WHY
Merge with transit data, weather data, etc.

content.definition: Problems of bias are often created by the type or source of data being collected. Bias is not eliminated by simply collecting more data — the source and collection method must be examined.

Large data sets are difficult to process using a single computer and may require parallel systems. The size of a data set affects the amount of information that can be extracted. Scalability of systems is an important consideration.

rows: Hospital studies general health using only wealthy urban clinic patients
More data from wealthy urban clinics still doesn't include rural or low-income patients
Collect from diverse clinics across income levels and geographies
Online poll used to predict election results
More online poll responses still only reach Internet-using, poll-participating demographics
Use stratified random sampling across all voter demographics
Facial recognition trained only on light-skinned faces
More light-skinned face photos don't add data for other skin tones
Collect training data representing all demographic groups proportionally

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Collecting MORE data from a biased source does NOT eliminate bias. If your data only comes from wealthy urban hospitals, collecting 10x more records from those same hospitals gives you 10x more biased data. The SOURCE must change. This is directly tested on the AP exam.
Topic 2.4 — Using Programs with Data

content.term: Four Ways to Extract or Modify Data Using a Program
content.definition:
1. Transforming — applying an operation to every element
2. Filtering — keeping only elements that meet a condition
3. Combining or comparing — such as finding the highest value
4. Visualizing — representing data through a chart or graph

rows: Transforming
Applies an operation to EVERY element in the data set
Doubling every revenue figure to project doubled sales; converting all temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit
Filtering
Keeps only elements that MEET A CONDITION — removes everything else
Keeping only students with GPA above 3.5; keeping only sales transactions above $1,000
Combining or comparing
Combines values or compares them to find summaries or relationships
Adding all sales to find total revenue; finding the student with the highest GPA; calculating the average temperature
Visualizing
Represents data through a chart, graph, or other visual
Bar chart of monthly sales; line graph of temperature over time; heat map of city congestion

content.definition: Search tools efficiently find information. Data filtering systems find patterns. Spreadsheets organize and find trends. Tables, diagrams, and visual tools communicate insights gained from data.

content.term: How do programs gain insight from data?
content.definition: Programs are used in an iterative and interactive way. Programmers can filter, clean, combine, cluster, classify, and transform data. Patterns can emerge when data are transformed using programs.

content.term: What does it mean to process data iteratively?
content.definition: Programs are used in an iterative and interactive way — meaning the programmer runs the program, examines the output, refines the approach, and runs it again. This cycle allows users to gradually gain deeper insight and knowledge from the data.

content.text: Combining data sources, clustering data, and classifying data are all parts of the process of using programs to gain insight and knowledge from data. Insight and knowledge can also be obtained from translating and transforming digitally represented information. Patterns can emerge when data are transformed using programs — patterns that would be impossible to see manually in large data sets.

rows: Combining data sources
Merging data from multiple sources into one data set
Combining sales data + customer location data + weather data to understand how weather affects purchases
Clustering data
Grouping similar data points together
Grouping customers by purchasing behavior to identify distinct buyer profiles for targeted marketing
Classifying data
Assigning data points to predefined categories
Classifying emails as spam or not spam based on content and sender patterns
Translating and transforming
Converting data into new forms to reveal meaning
Translating audio to text; converting raw sensor readings to human-readable temperature values

content.text: Connecting the Topics: How Unit 2 Fits Together
The four topics in Unit 2 tell a complete story about data — from how it is stored at the lowest level all the way up to how programs extract knowledge from it.

rows: How is data stored?
2.1 Binary Numbers
Everything is bits. Bits group to represent numbers, characters, color, and more. The same bits mean different things in different contexts.
How is data made smaller?
2.2 Data Compression
Lossless removes redundancy without losing data. Lossy removes data to achieve greater reduction. Choice depends on whether exact reconstruction matters.
What can data tell us?
2.3 Extracting Information
Data reveals trends, correlations, and patterns. Correlation ≠ causation. Data must be cleaned, combined from multiple sources, and checked for bias.
How do programs help?
2.4 Using Programs with Data
Programs transform, filter, combine, and visualize data iteratively to extract information. Patterns emerge that would be impossible to find manually.
